newsitem.title: USA: U.S. voter turnout lowest in any presidential race.
newsitem.headline: U.S. voter turnout lowest in any presidential race.

text.p: President Bill Clinton won the 1996 presidential election with less than half the vote in a year when voter turnout fell below 50 percent for the first time in a presidential election.

In Tuesday's voting, Clinton became the first Democrat to win re-election to the White House since Franklin Roosevelt in 1944. With more than 99 percent of the vote counted, Clinton received 49.2 percent of the vote to 40.8 percent for Republican Bob Dole and 8.5 percent for third-party candidate Ross Perot.

But voting returns showed that the percentage of registered voters who went to the polls fell to a record low of 49 percent. The next-lowest turnout was recorded in 1988, when 50.15 percent voted as Republican George Bush defeated Democrat Michael Dukakis.
The third-lowest turnout was the 51.3 percent of 1948, when Democrat Harry Truman beat Republican Thomas E. Dewey.
Clinton defeated Bush in 1992 with a voter turnout of 55.23 percent, according to the Federal Election Commission.

Curtis Gans of the Committee for the Study of the American Electorate, a voter analysis group, deplored the decline in voter interest, which he blamed partly on "anti-government demagoguery" which discouraged people from voting.
Ellen Shearer, co-director of the Medill News Service of the graduate programme at Northwestern University, said that "90 million Americans not voting means that almost an elite chooses our leaders.
"It's scary that now children of non-voters are not voting," she said.
The Medill News Service has been studying why Americans choose to stay home and this year it surveyed over 1,000 likely non-voters. Its study came to some surprising conclusions.

One was that 29 percent of the total consisted of what Shearer dubs "the doers," affluent, college-educated people who follow the news closely. "They just don't think they need to vote," she said. She attributed their feeling to satisfaction with their personal finances.

A second group of 27 percent, whom Shearer calls "the unplugged," were younger and less affluent people who hold a negative view of the government and think the issues in the election do not relate to them.
"Irritables" account for 18 percent. Shearer said these were affluent, generally older people who are very sceptical about politics and do not like what is going on politically.
About 14 percent of those surveyed were "don't knows," who have no opinions on political issues and have left politics to others to deal with.

The rest were "the alienated," people who are very negative toward politics and generally over 45 years of age. Unlike "the irritables," they pay remarkably little attention to what is happening politically, Shearer said.
